title: The market and the law
summary: Who gets sued, who pays back, and what a careful buyer checks — from Knoedler to the Cologne courts and Germany's highest civil court in 2026.

shots.title:
Who pays when
the experts are wrong?
shots.narration: Forgery is a crime, but much of the fight happens in civil courts and sale rooms. This lesson follows the money: who gets sued, who pays back, and what a careful buyer checks.
Markets create forgeries. When an artist's prices climb at auction, or a major study is published, many previously unknown works can suddenly appear for sale.

shots.text: One of New York's oldest galleries **closed in 2011**.
shots.narration: Knoedler and Company, one of New York's oldest and most reputable galleries, closed in 2011 after being accused of selling forged Abstract Expressionist paintings.

shots.heading: Red flags the buyers said were ignored
items: So many works from one source
shots.narration: Buyers argued the gallery ignored red flags: the number of works, the huge profit margins and the mysterious provenance. Its director said the experts she consulted believed the works genuine.

shots.label: million dollars forfeited by the dealer **Glafira Rosales**
shots.context: Guilty plea in Manhattan federal court, September 2013.
shots.narration: The works' source, the dealer Glafira Rosales, pleaded guilty in September 2013 to charges including wire fraud and money laundering, and agreed to forfeit 33.2 million dollars.

shots.text: A basement cache **no one could find**.
shots.narration: Between 2005 and 2014, John Re sold dozens of fake Pollocks and de Koonings with a story about a basement cache. IFAR found no evidence for it, and in November 2014 he pleaded guilty to wire fraud.

shots.text: Deceived, in good faith — and **still liable**.
shots.narration: In Germany, a Cologne court ordered the auction house that sold Beltracchi's fake Campendonk to pay the buyer back about 2.1 million euros — although it had been deceived too, and acted in good faith.

shots.text: The catalogue said **'certain'** without the evidence.
shots.narration: The reason: its catalogue presented the attribution as certain without a sufficient factual basis. It had neither checked the consignor's provenance nor had the painting examined.

The case isn't over. On 9 October 2026 Germany's Federal Court of Justice heard the forger's claim to recover the painting after the sale was unwound and it was resold. Lower courts rejected it; a ruling is due in January.

shots.text: Intent turns a copy **into a forgery**.
shots.narration: Copies are not crimes in themselves: curators treat the intent to deceive as central. John Myatt now sells 'genuine fakes', each clearly signed so it can never pass as authentic.

Mark Landis gave fakes to dozens of museums for about thirty years. They lost no money and he claimed no tax deductions, so he technically committed no fraud. He stopped in 2014, after media attention.

shots.heading: Before you buy
items: Trace the provenance in independent records
Ask: why this work, why now, from whom?
Get the seller's claims in writing
shots.narration: So before you buy: trace the provenance in independent records, commission a scientific examination, search the stolen-art databases, ask why this work is appearing now — and get the seller's claims in writing.
In this lesson's cases, the evidence that exposed the fakes — a modern pigment, an invented collector, a cache no one could find — could have been looked for before the sale.

steps.title: Go deeper: lessons from Knoedler
steps.caption: '20/20 Hindsight: Lessons from the Knoedler/Rosales Affair', a programme from the International Foundation for Art Research (IFAR), whose research on the John Re case features in this lesson.

steps.title: Red flag or reassurance?
steps.brief: You're advising a buyer. Sort what the seller offers: a **red flag**, **neutral on its own**, or **reassuring — if verified at source**.

cards.text: Dozens of never-exhibited works, all from one source
cards.why: Volume from a single, unexplained source was one of the flags in the Knoedler case.

cards.text: A seller who won't name the previous owner
A wave of 'new' works just after a record auction price
cards.why: High prices are exactly when previously unknown works start to appear.

cards.text: A gallery label on the back of the frame
cards.why: Labels are easy to make — Beltracchi's fakes carried labels of a collection that never held them.

cards.text: A clean search in INTERPOL's stolen-art database
cards.why: It shows the work isn't registered as stolen. It says nothing about whether it is authentic.

cards.text: An old sale catalogue listing the work with matching size and subject
cards.why: Independent records that match the object are the backbone of provenance — if you check the catalogue in a library, since archives have been doctored.

cards.text: A pre-sale materials report from an independent laboratory
cards.why: It's the check the Cologne auction house never made. Remember that consistent materials show only that a work could be old.

questions.prompt: Why did a Cologne court order the auction house to repay the buyer, although it had been deceived too?
options: Its catalogue presented the attribution as certain without a sufficient factual basis
It had refused to return the buyer's deposit
questions.explain: The court also noted it had neither checked the provenance nor had the painting examined.

questions.prompt: Which of these was NOT among the red flags Knoedler's buyers said the gallery ignored?
options: A lab report finding a modern pigment
questions.explain: The buyers pointed to volume, margins and provenance — warnings visible without a laboratory.

questions.prompt: What do curators treat as central to a forgery, as opposed to a copy?
questions.explain: Myatt's signed 'genuine fakes' are legal because no one is deceived.

questions.prompt: What did Germany's Federal Court of Justice hear in October 2026?
options: A new criminal charge against the forger
The forger's claim to get the painting back
questions.explain: Lower courts had rejected the claim; the ruling is scheduled for January.
